projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harold Cowey was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I enlisted

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Rochester New York

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: When did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: January 1939 in the National Guard, I was called to active duty in October 1940

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you choose what branch you wanted to be in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yes. I joined to play basketball

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: That's always a good reason

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It is really (laughs)

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Where did you get your training?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Fort McCleanlin Alabama

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was your unit all from the same area?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: yes all from Rochester

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Which wars were you in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: WW2 and Korea

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Where were you in those wars?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Pacific Ocean.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What battles were you in? HarokLGuata Canal, New Guinea, New Britain, and the Philippines

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What unit were you in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: 108th Infentry, and the 6th Ranger battalion

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So you were a Ranger?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yep

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Sergeant

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever meet any generals?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah I met a lot of generals...

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Which ones?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: MacArthur, two or three times, General Rice, a couple of others I can't remember their names now...

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was anybody in your unit ever captured?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Captured? No

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did your unit ever receive heavy casualties?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah, a lot of em. Well 70 percent.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Would you eventually get stuck in a different group? Or did they just in new people?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Replacements

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were you awarded any metals?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah I got a couple purple heart, and bronze star

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How were the communications between you and the States?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: what do you mean, between me and the US? Intervieweryeah, were you able to send letters back?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah, we sent V-mail

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: what was V-mail?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: well you'd write a regular letter, they'd put it on microfilm and send it back to the States, the they'd reprint it

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: how long did it take to get those back?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: A couple months, sometimes

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well, I won't eat that kind of food now, I can tell you that. K-rations weren't too bad the C-rations sucked.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was the difference?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: C-Rations came in a can, you just warmed em up.. Hash, beans, And something else I can't remember the other one now. K-rations were pretty good, they had crackers in em, though they were a little stale, they had cocoa that you could warm up with water and powdered milk, powdered cereal, powdered eggs, all in a little box. The best rations were a ten in one. Ten people for one day.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How often did you get those, like once a week or every day...?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: you'd get three or four meals at a time and that was it. some times you didn't get'em for three or four days. You didn't eat every day. Depends where you were, in the rear you got fed every day if you were on the line you got fed when they could get to you.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever work with civilians?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Civilians? Yeah, in the Philippines

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they American civilians, or?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: A couple Filipino scouts with us, they were civilians but they were well Filipino scouts, but technically civilians they weren't in any army

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What did people do for fun there?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well, if you weren't fighting. If you weren't on front lines you played baseball, basketball, stuff like that in the rear areas. Swimming a lot of swimming, we were always on islands and surrounded by water. So most of the people were swimming most of the time. We saw shows once in a while, band concerts once in a while we had USO come around, I saw Bob Hope

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Who was Bob Hope?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: He was a comedian he died about a hundred years old he was. A big hollywood movie star. I saw others Kenny Granny, a lot of hollywood stars came around in the USO shows

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did any of the stars join the military?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: well yeah a lot of movie stars joined the army, Ronald Regean a president was in the army, Jimmy Stewart was in the army, Ted Williams was in the army, wait he was in the marines he fought as a fighter pilot in WW2 and again in Korea.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever interact with any of the other military groups?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well the navy is the one that took us places. We went every place by boat so we used navy ships. And we worked a lot with the air force, they covered us, so did the navy. With fighter planes and bombers. Never worked with the marines.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they a big group back then?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well yeah they were just as big as the army, there was more in the army. They had more men in the army. The marines operated by themselves, the marines were run by the navy, they are part of the navy

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: When did your service end in WW2?

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How long did it take you to get back to the united states after that?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: ! was on the way back when the war ended, I was coming back on rotation.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So you didn't go back in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: No I got discharged. The war got over in Europe in may 1945, and the war ended in Japan in August of 1945. I had enough points to get out, in June of 1945

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How did the point system work?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well you got so many points for every month you served, so many point for every month over seas, so many points for every ribbon you got, medals you got. I had more than enough you only needed 90 points I had 135.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you get your education through the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I went to school on it yeah.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It would pay for your college education, and you got a break if you bought a house. I used it on both.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: When did you rejoin for Korea?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: October 1946. I went back in the National Guard I got inducted in to active duty in September 1950 got discharged in October 1951

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What were you in in Korea?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I was in an ordinance company

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What did the ordinance company do?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We maintained all the equipment. Mostly vehicles and weapons.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: When you were rejoined for Korea were you still in the army?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: No I was civilian from June 1945 to 1946

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What did you do while you were a civilian?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I worked for Kodak for a while. In the Distillation products

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What are distillation products? Harold'.It made vitamins

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever meet any Japanese prisoners?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: yeah

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever interact with them at all?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Not any more than I had to

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did the civilians that were liberated from the Japanese, did they like America?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Most were. Most couldn't speak english though. Most were natives there weren't any Caucasian civilians in most of the places. Till we got to the Philippines. The Filipinos were very good. They were glad the Americans came back.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you deal with any American prisoners that had been taken by the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah, Katatauan, out side of Manilla

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How had they been treated?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: They were all skinny, under weight, sick, most had some form of a disease

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever interact with them?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well I talked to some of them but they all went to the hospitals and medics

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you do mostly amphibious assaults?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: yeah we made two beach landings. In New Britain and the Philippines, in the Legan Gulf in the Philippines

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Which was first?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: When we went to Guata Canal there were already us troops there. We went in by small boats, but the island already had Americans on it. When we went to New Britain in the Philippines there were no American soldiers there

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So you were the first group in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We were the first wave yeah

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were there any others were you were the first in?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well no, but that didn't mean any thing, fighting was still heavy on the others

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you ever build airfields on any of the islands?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: That was usually done by CB's

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What are CB's?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: They belonged to the navy, they were Construction Battalions, they did most of the airfields. There was already an airfield on the Philippines, it had been an army base before the war started Interviewer.How large was your unit?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It went from 260 down to 30 men at one time.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How long were you at 30 men?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Probably 3 or 4 weeks, they pulled you out of the line or put you in a different unit

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were you ever wounded?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well some pieces hit me, but nothing serious

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Do you remember what medals you got?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well I got a Bronze Star

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was that for?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well just for valor. I could dig a hole deeper than anyone else

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How many people in your unit made it through the whole war?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: When I left I think there were 12 of us left

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was it common to get moved to another unit?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well the army works funny. If there is a unit on the line and it gets pulled off and another unit gets put in, sometimes they'll take men out of your unit and put em in with the new unit going on the line.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they usually the higher ups?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: No any body, if they need a lieutenant they'll move one in, if they need 20 privates they'll take 20 privates from reserves

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was your unit mostly enlisted or draftees?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well by the time we went overseas it was 50/50

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did that changes towards the end?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah by the end it was mostly draftees

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was your first job in the army?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: ! was any infantryman

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you receive any specialty training?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah because I was in a machine-gun company

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So was everyone a heavy machine-gunner in your company?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well we had 2 thirty-cal guns, one 181 mm mortar,

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How big is a company?

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How many are in a platoon?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well it depends. Each platoon had 4 squads in it. We had 10 men squads. 2 machine-gun squads and a mortar squad, and a squad of extra men'. We had a fifty-cal platoon two of em plus truck divers cooks and others. But every one could fight

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What did you think of the officers?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: The officers were good, most of em. We had some ROTC officers which got to be officers by going to college.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they better than the regular officers?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It depends on when you got em. Some had been in active duty for a while others hadn't. They didn't know much. Most officers when they first got in a unit they didn't know much. They left stuff up to the sergeants. They knew the book work, but they didn't have training in ducking.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were any of the officers from WW1?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: No some of the generals maybe

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How many sergeants to privates were there?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: 220 privates 8 officers and about 20 corporals and sergeants. Probably 10:1 ten privates to every sergeant

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was artillery accurate?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: They call it saturation fire they fire sequentially across the field, and any thing in there got shot

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So was it good for clearing areas?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: There would still be enemy there. They would go in holes or caves. You couldn't close up all the caves, tanks would try and do that

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What do you mean by close off do you mean just wall up the caves?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well you'd have a big hole on the side of the mountain or hill, and they'd bring up a tank and shoot into the hole and try and close it up. A lot of times the had four or five openings to the cave. You couldn't close em all up

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Do you remember any military oddities?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well when we were in the Philippines we had aa guy come by a six o'clock every night in an air plane, it sounded like it was on two cylinders, he would drop one bomb and run away, every one would stand out and laugh at him

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was he an enemy?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah, he was Japanese. Charlie six we used to call him came every night at six o'clock. He would be sputtering away, he would drop one bomb never hit any thing, he could have been shot down several times but everyone just laughed at him, he was in an old biplane. But nobody paid him any attention after a while.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Do you remember what the most feared enemy weapon was?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Probably their machine-guns, then they had 20 mm cannons they took which were anti aircraft guns at Clark's field at the Philippines they'd hide them in caves up there they'dbring em out at night you could see the tracers coming at you. They were always flying high.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you have to deal with kamikaze attacks?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah I saw a Australian cruiser get hit by one, The Cambrial. They sunk it in the harbor at Legan Gulf. And I saw an aircraft carrier get hit but it wasn't hurt too bad

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you deal a lot with foreign troops?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We had some Australians, those were the only foreign troops we saw. We called em Anzac. Australia and New Zealand put together. They were good fighters

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they integrated with you?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: They had their own units but they were with us. They fought next to us a couple of times.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How long was your training period?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well I didn't have to go to much training, because I was in the National Guard. But the first draftees was in January 1941, and they got 6 weeks basic training.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was included in basic training?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Marksmanship, infantry tactics,firing range

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they well prepared for combat?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well by the time they got done with their 6 weeks they were

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was there any thing you had to learn once you got into real combat?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Keep low, duck

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were there any tactics that they taught you that just didn't work?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well we're different, we find an area of ground and cover the area and just shoot the guns. We didn't have to get up and charge or anything, like the riflemen do. A weapon company covers them. You try to get on high ground. You put the guns so they cover everything in front. So nobody can get through the firing. Field of fire they call it. Then you had mortars dropping in between

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So you didn't have to do any close combat then?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Yeah we did close fighting. Ten feet close enough for you? Scary

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was it common for that to happen to happen or was

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It happened four or five time. At Guadalcanal it happened and at New Britain and New Guinea it happened and at the Philippines it happened too. They'd charge what you do. You don't move, you stay there

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So it was never you moving forward it was the enemy coming at you?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: well no we moved forward too,the infantry would go up and take one hill we would have to go up to the next hill, but we didn't charge the enemy HaroldT got some thing for you, did you study about Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Yeah

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I got a new paper at home shows the whole attack of Pearl out of a regular Democrat and Chronicle, you can barrow it if you want to

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How soon after Pear Harbor were you put into active duty?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We went over seas January 9th 1942 and pearl was December 7th 1942 so it was a month and two days, I was in Fort McCleanlin Alabama when the war started. I was at Hupwhiler Hotel Birmingham Alabama, throwing bags of water out the window, at the pedestrians on the street when the war started. They was all dressed up going to church. There was six of us there.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they all from your unit

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We were on break it was the week end so. We went to Birmingham, the largest city where we were, and we didn't have any thing to do so we filled paper bags with water and dropped em out the window

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: You said you had leave so how did the national guard work did you have to show up at certain times?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We drilled once a week, and then we went two weeks summer camp

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: SO how long had you been in the national guard before the war started?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well I joined in January 39, sent to active duty in October 1940, so almost two years

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How old were you when you joined?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: 17 I lied about my age

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was it common for minors to join? HarokhWell seriously I Joined to play basketball. Seriously I did.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: So you didn't think a war was coming?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Oh no. not in 1940, they had the basketball team in rochester, at the armory. And they went around and played teams all over. Well a fellow I went to high school with, already joined he was two years older than me. He talked me in to joining just to play basketball. When I joined you got paid a dollar a drill

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was that good pay?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well a dollar a day was a lot of money those days. I only worked one day a week

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was there an hourly wage minimum then

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: No, that was big pay in those days

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What could a dollar buy then

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well a lot of things. Bread was 10 cents a loaf. I was back in the thirties, the depression was still on

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was it mostly over by then?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well no the depression wasn't over until the war started. It was starting to decline a little, but it was still going. The stock market closed in 1929 that's when everything fell apart. There were people selling apples on the corner for a nickel a piece. A lot of people didn't even work in the twenties. There was no such thing as welfare. Nobody had money

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did your family have work?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well my father worked a streetcar, some days he didn't work at all, some days he would work two hours, some days he would work all day

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was a streetcar like a taxi?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well it was like a bus. He was an extra, he would go down and sit in the car barn, where the trolleys were kept, and wait for one to break down or some times they would need an extra one like if there was a ball game. He might only take one run that day. If they didn't call him or nothing broke down he wouldn't work at all.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was that a good job for the time?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well he was steadily employed. He got paid 50 cents a hour some only got paid 20 cents an hour, nobody made more than 50 cents an hour

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: For that period was your family living well?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well we weren't starving and we had a place to live, and clothes, but only two sets, a good pair and good cloths. For Christmas we always got cloths.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you go to school? Harold-.yeah, I graduated

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Did you leave school to join the guard?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well you didn't have to it was only on the week ends and summer

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What was your action for the bronze star?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: ! got that in the Philippines

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: For anything in specific?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: You get recommended for it. Well a jap tank came from around a hill. We were on the front of the hill. They started firing at us every body ran but me and I set it on fire

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: When you said you set it on fire?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We had tracer bullets, they are incendiary, and the tank had cameo on it and when the bullets hi the cameo it started to burn. They turned around the corner and BOOM. I was young and foolish, I wouldn't do it to day. I would have been the first one down the back of the hill today.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Was it common to run into jap tanks?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Oh yeah on the Philippines

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: But on the small islands they didn't have them?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well yeah, mostly small ones

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: How was your air support?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: We had great air support the navy was greatest

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Once you called it in how long did it take?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: WelL it depended on where they were. Sometime you would get it in thirty seconds, there was always planes flying up there. It just depended what they were loaded with, some times they were fighters or dive bombers sometimes they were torpedo planes. They could always come and strafe. But sometimes it could take a while, they would have already been on a mission and be going home, didn't have any bullets left. I never saw any big bombers though. Like B-17.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: Were they mostly in europe?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Well, they were around but I never saw them. I mean where I was in Hawaii I saw them, B-24, they were heavy bombers just like a B-17. The marines were fighting on Okinawa at the same time we were fighting, that's were they sent the B-29s

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: I even got a good conduct medal

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: For being good

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: You got a medal for doing what you were told?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: Basically I didn't shoot any officers, They wouldn't give your mother a good conduct medal.

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
sp.p: What did you think of Private Ryan?

sp.speaker: Harold Cowey
sp.p: It was good, I was crying in that movie

sp.speaker: Justin Woodward
